userJob: Decide whether a component should be written at all
problem: Every piece of the design becomes a new component, so the project grows a private version of a control the browser already ships and each one has to re-earn focus, keyboard and screen reader behaviour
worksWhen: Before writing any component, on every build
avoidWhen: Never; the ladder is four questions and answering them is faster than the component
mechanism: Climb four rungs before writing anything. Does it need to exist at all. Is it already in this codebase. Can the platform do it natively. And if you add a dependency, name the native API it replaces. Where a browser control exists for the job, use it, because a rebuilt control has to re-earn focus, keyboard and screen reader behaviour and the verification gate will find out.
risks: Rebuilding select, dialog, details or date input for appearance, which trades a styling problem for an accessibility one
Detecting existing components by name rather than by behaviour, so a near-match is adopted and then forked
mobileRules: Native controls bring the platform's own mobile behaviour, including the correct keyboard and picker; a rebuilt control brings none of it
accessibilityRules: A rebuilt control needs focus management, keyboard operation, roles, states and announcement, all of which the native one already has
Anything that reads as operable is operable
genericnessNote: Using the platform's control does not decide how it is styled, and the styling still comes from the direction.

userJob: Decide whether a group of content needs a card around it
problem: Every group gets a bordered, rounded, shadowed container, so the page becomes a grid of boxes and the boxes carry no hierarchy of their own
worksWhen: Elevation communicates something real: this thing is above the page, is dismissible, is a separate surface
avoidWhen: The grouping is only conceptual, where space and a rule do the same work without adding a frame
mechanism: Use cards ONLY when elevation communicates real hierarchy. Otherwise group with border-t, divide-y, or negative space.
risks: Nested cards, where a card inside a card claims two levels of elevation that do not exist
A card used to hide inconsistent content heights, which is a layout problem wearing a container
mobileRules: At 375px a card's padding and border eat measurable width; check the measure inside the card, not only outside it
accessibilityRules: A card that is entirely clickable is one focusable target, not a container with three overlapping links
If the card is a region, give it a heading rather than only a visual border
genericnessNote: Card grids are the default answer to any set, so removing the container is usually the more specific decision.

userJob: Build the states a component has beyond its successful one
problem: Only the populated success state is built, so empty, loading, partial and error appear first in production and are designed by whoever is on call
worksWhen: Any component that renders data it did not create
avoidWhen: Never; a component with unreachable states is unfinished, not simple
mechanism: Empty, loading, error and partial are all built and all reachable in the running page. Partial ranks with the others: a half-succeeded bulk action says which half. Empty states are an invitation rather than an apology, and error states say what happened and what to do about it.
risks: Building the states but leaving no route to them, so nobody has ever seen them render
A loading state whose shape does not match the loaded one, which shows as a jump
mobileRules: Each state is checked at 375px; empty states with illustrations are the ones that overflow
An error that appears above the fold on desktop can appear below it on mobile
accessibilityRules: State changes are announced, not only rendered
An empty state is readable text, not an image of text
Error text meets 4.5:1 and is bound to the thing that failed
genericnessNote: Requiring the states says nothing about their form, and the copy in them comes from the subject's voice.

userJob: Place actions so nothing has to be held in memory on the way to them
problem: Row actions live in a toolbar at the top, so the operator selects a row, travels to the toolbar, and has to remember which row they chose
worksWhen: Listings, records, forms and any surface where actions apply to a specific object
avoidWhen: A genuinely global action such as export or refresh, which belongs at the surface level
mechanism: Row actions on the row, form actions at the end of the form. Destructive actions are separated from constructive ones by position rather than only by colour, and are either undoable or confirmed by a sentence naming what will be lost. A disabled control says why, or it is not disabled.
risks: A destructive action adjacent to the most-used one, where position separation was replaced by a red tint
Disabling a control with no explanation, which reads as a broken interface
mobileRules: At 375px row actions usually collapse into a menu; the destructive entry stays separated inside that menu too
44px targets with 24px clearance, which constrains how many row actions can be inline
accessibilityRules: Every row action is reachable by keyboard, and the key is shown on screen
A destructive confirmation names what will be lost in its own text, not only in a heading
A disabled control exposes its reason to assistive technology as well as visually
genericnessNote: Placing actions at their object is a structural rule that different working units express differently.

userJob: Lay out a single form field's parts
problem: Label, helper and error each land wherever the component author put them, so a form built from several components has three different field anatomies
worksWhen: Every form field on every surface
avoidWhen: A single search field in a toolbar, where a visible label may sit outside the field group; the accessible name is still required
mechanism: Label ABOVE input. Helper text optional but present in markup. Error text BELOW input. Standard gap-2 for input blocks.
risks: Helper text present in markup but hidden by default, which hides it from everyone rather than only visually
Error text inserted rather than revealed, which shifts the field as validation runs
mobileRules: Label above rather than beside, because beside costs the input its width at 375px
Reserve the error line's height so the field does not move
accessibilityRules: The label is bound to the input by for and id
Helper and error text are associated with the input so they are announced with it
No placeholder-as-label, ever
genericnessNote: Field anatomy is structural; the type, spacing and colour of the parts remain the design's own.

userJob: Give a control a pressed state that feels physical without shifting layout
problem: Controls have a hover state and nothing on press, so on touch there is no feedback at all and the user taps twice
worksWhen: Buttons, tappable cards and any control with a discrete commit
avoidWhen: Controls near money, where the answer is the control rewriting its own word rather than moving
mechanism: Tactile Feedback: On :active, use -translate-y-[1px] or scale-[0.98] to simulate a physical push.
risks: Scaling a control that contains text small enough to blur during the transform
Using a transform large enough to move adjacent content visually, which reads as a layout bug
mobileRules: Visual feedback within about 100ms of the tap
The transform must not move the target out from under the finger
accessibilityRules: The keyboard focus state is separate from and at least as visible as the press state
Under reduced motion the press state is a discrete change rather than a transition
genericnessNote: A one-pixel push is a mechanism, and the control's whole appearance is still the design's.

userJob: Present more than a handful of items without a long ruled list
problem: A set of fifteen items becomes a fifteen-row list with a hairline under every row, which is the laziest possible layout and reads as a data dump
worksWhen: Sets past about five items on a page whose job is not to be a table
avoidWhen: A genuine data table an operator sorts and scans, where rows and rules are the right component
mechanism: Past about five items, reach for a component rather than a longer list: a two-column split with grouped items, a card grid with an image per item, tabs or an accordion when the items are categorisable, horizontal scroll-snap pills, or a marquee when the items do not need individual attention. Where a specification really must be shown whole, group it into a few clusters with sparse dividers rather than ruling every row.
risks: Hiding items behind an accordion that nobody opens, which removes the content rather than presenting it
A carousel for items the reader needs to compare, which makes comparison impossible
mobileRules: Horizontal scroll-snap groups scroll inside their own container, never the document
Tabs at 375px need a visible indication that further tabs exist off-screen
accessibilityRules: Tabs and accordions carry their roles, states and keyboard behaviour, or they are not tabs and accordions
A scroll-snap group is reachable and traversable by keyboard
A grouped specification is still a real table or definition list with headers
genericnessNote: The alternatives listed are themselves common components, so the choice has to follow from what the items are rather than from the count alone.

userJob: Use an installed component library without shipping the library's design
problem: Components are installed and used at their defaults, so the page is the vendor's design and so is every other site that installed it
worksWhen: Any project using a component library, a starter kit or generated blocks
avoidWhen: A named design system the brief asked for by name, where the system's own appearance is the requirement
mechanism: Anything generated or vendored is restyled from the direction's own token layer before it ships. At default styling it is the vendor's design. Restyling means radii, colour, shadow and type mapped onto the project's tokens, not one override on the primary button.
risks: Overriding at the component rather than at the token layer, so the next component reverts
Mixing two design systems in one project, which produces two visual languages arguing
mobileRules: Vendor defaults often assume a desktop density; check target sizes and spacing at 375px after restyling
accessibilityRules: Restyling must not lower the contrast the vendor's defaults happened to satisfy
Focus indicators are commonly the first thing a restyle removes; verify the indicator meets contrast on its own
genericnessNote: Default-styled libraries are the single most reliable route to a page that looks like every other page built this year.

userJob: Tell whether a screen or a menu is overloaded
problem: Density is judged by feel, so a screen that is overloaded to a first-time user reads as fine to the person who built it
worksWhen: Any decision point: a navigation bar, a filter panel, a set of same-weight controls, a first screen
avoidWhen: A deliberately dense reference surface an expert scans daily, where the count is the content
mechanism: At any decision point, count the visible interactive options, the top-level navigation entries, and the competing same-weight elements. Four or fewer is manageable, five to seven is the boundary, eight or more is overloaded. Counting replaces judgement, which is what makes the check survive familiarity with the design.
risks: Reducing the count by hiding options behind a menu, which moves the problem rather than solving it
Counting only buttons and missing same-weight links, cards and controls that compete for the same decision
mobileRules: Count against the 375px view, where collapsed navigation and stacked controls change what competes with what
accessibilityRules: Options moved behind a disclosure remain reachable by keyboard and announce their expanded state
genericnessNote: A count is a measurement and produces different answers for different content.
